newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE - Long road to privatising Israel defence firms.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Long road to privatising Israel defence firms.

text.p: Workers at Israel's biggest government-owned defence company had a surprise for their chairman when he visited one of their factories this year.
All 400 employees of Israel Aircraft Industries' Ramta plant in dusty Beersheba quietly left their stations and walked out to protest at efforts by management to privatise the company.

Powerful labour unions and nagging security considerations have nudged government-owned defence companies, burdened by years of heavy losses, to the bottom of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's list of firms for sale.

"A company that operates on the scale of Israel Aircraft Industries and with the array of military and civilian deals it does, must be run like a financial company in every respect," said Doron Suslik, IAI's director of corporate communications.
"For this reason, it should not be in the government sector," he told Reuters.

Netanyahu has vowed to sell off 50 government-owned companies in four years. Aides say his government hopes by next year to take initial steps towards privatising parts of IAI or bringing in strategic investors but some analysts say it's a mission impossible.

"This government doesn't have the guts to take such a hard, complicated and potentially unpopular step as privatising the defence industries," Amnon Barzilai, defence analyst of the newspaper Haaretz, told Reuters.
NO MORE GOVERNMENT BAIL-OUTS
IAI is the flagship of a defence industry built to provide military self-sufficiency for a country at war with its neighbours.

Financial losses incurred over the years were seen as the price Israel must pay for its edge in everything from radars to tanks and ballistic missiles. Founders never dreamt the government would one day want to sell it.
But in the last five years alone the government has had to fork over nearly $1 billion for IAI's recovery, a figure some analysts say is not far from the company's market value.
The financial situation at the smaller Israel Military Industries and Rafael, the other two government-owned defences companies, is also troubled.
The treasury, already burdened by a spiralling budget deficit, has vowed no more bail-outs.

"I have no doubt that the (defence) industries fully understand they can no longer count on subsidies or additional recovery programmes," Defence Ministry Director-General Ilan Biran said in an interview with the financial daily Globes.

Management expects IAI will turn a profit in 1997 for the first time in years, projecting earnings of $22 million on $1.62 billion in sales compared with a $40 million loss last year, according to defence sources.

But domestic orders have steadily declined as the Jewish state edges closer to peace with its neighbours. Defence spending accounts this year for about 16 percent of Israel's budget compared with an average 24 percent in much of the 1980s.
Abroad, Israeli firms have had to contend with post-Cold War political trends that have ailed defence industries worldwide, and stiff competition.
WORKERS HOLD THE KEY

The chairman of IAI's board of directors, Avigdor Ben-Gal, has talked since his appointment last year about a restructuring process within the company -- which includes 14 divisions -- that would put it on a path to recovery and eventually to privatisation.
But the word is anathema to workers, who fear privatisation means salary cuts and massive layoffs.
"Privatisation is suddenly trendy. Show me one example of privatisation that was good for the workers," said Chaim Katz, 50, head of a committee representing IAI's nearly 15,000 workers.
"No one can go over our heads to privatise this company. The management here can't do a thing without our agreement," he told Reuters.
Collective agreements IAI has signed over the years testify to employees' strength.

Under the agreements, dismissing workers or redefining their positions in any restructuring plan is nearly impossible. Katz said the agreement also conditions the sale of all or part of IAI on prior consent of the workers.
"This could make it very difficult or very expensive to privatise IAI," said a finance official involved in efforts to restructure the company.
He said Israel could end up paying workers a huge portion of the money it would get in the sale of IAI to obtain their consent.
"In essence, they hold the key," said the finance official, who refused to be identified.
THE "WHIMS OF A PRIVATE COMPANY"
Katz said management officials had not contacted him over the issue. One reason might be that nobody knows yet how much of IAI will be privatised and how the process will be implemented.

Israel will want to maintain control over whole sections that it views as vital to its security, such as the Malam plant where the Shavit missile is manufactured and where the Arrow missile is being developed.
It will also want to maintain a golden share wherever arms and ammunition are manufactured.
"We would not want to put ourselves in a situation where we have to rely on the whims of a private company to supply us with everything we need if a war suddenly erupts," said the finance official.
Officials must also decide if parts of the company would be sold to investors or offered to the public.
"The owner of the company, which is the Israeli government, must decide its policy on a whole string of issues," Suslik said.
EYEING THE NEXT ELECTION
Analysts agree the more conditions Israel attaches to the sale, the harder it will be to find a buyer for IAI and the other defence firms.
But politics could prove to be the ultimate obstacle.
IAI workers have strong ties with the unions of other government-owned companies and together employees and their families account for enough votes to put several legislators in parliament.
The closer Israel gets to its next election in 2000 the less willing the government will be to face labour unrest and alienate voters.
"In a democratic regime, if you don't make difficult decisions in the first year, you won't make them in the second or third year," said Barzilai of the Haaretz newspaper.

"Even if the first steps towards privatisation are taken now, nothing serious will happen until 1999 and with an election year around the corner, no government wants to make unpopular moves," he said.
